entries.narration: Machine learning is worth reaching for when a relationship is too tangled to write down as rules, but examples of it are sitting in your data. Our running example is a fictional retailer that wants to know, at the moment a customer checks out, how long the delivery will take and whether it will arrive late. Those are supervised problems: there is a target we eventually observe, minutes to the door, or late versus on time, and we learn a mapping from what we know at checkout to that target. The same data also supports unsupervised questions, where there is no target at all: which customers behave alike, how to compress many features into a few, which orders look unusual. But before any of that, write down the baseline. The carrier already publishes a promised-days table, and the median delivery time per zone is one line of code. A model has to beat that bar on the same evaluation, by enough to justify what it costs to build and run. If the rule already decides well, learning only adds risk.

Every model in this course starts from a contract, and it is worth writing down before touching any data. The unit is one order, not one customer and not one day, so each row we learn from is an order. The target for the first task is the number of minutes from checkout to the doorstep. For the second, an order is late if it arrives after the promise we showed at checkout, which means the promise itself is fixed at that moment too. The prediction time is the checkout click, and that single point on the order's timeline does a lot of work: anything that happens afterwards, dispatch, the courier's route, the actual delivery, simply does not exist yet, so it cannot be a feature. Finally, name the decision the prediction changes: the promise displayed to the customer, or whether to offer an express upgrade. The contract also states the claim. Do we mean future orders, unseen customers, or both? Those imply different splits, and the next chapter depends on that answer.

Once the contract is fixed, every column in the orders table gets exactly one role. Features are what the model is allowed to see, and the test is simple: was this value known at the checkout click? The delivery zone, the number of items in the basket, the distance, and the promise we displayed all pass. The target is what we are learning to predict, duration in minutes for one task and the late flag for the other. Notice that late is derived from duration and the promise, so it can never also be a feature. Everything else is metadata: the order id, the customer id, the timestamp. Metadata is not junk to discard. The customer id is how we will keep whole customers out of training when the claim is about new customers. The timestamp is how we order rows in time and enforce the cutoff. What metadata must never become is a feature. An id carries no general pattern, so a model that sees it can memorise individual rows, and that looks like accuracy until it meets an order it has never seen.

A label is only as good as the moment it was taken. The curve on the left shows, for orders of each age, what share has actually been delivered. Look at three days: about half of those orders are still in transit. Their duration is not short, it is unknown. If we train on recent orders and keep only the ones that have already arrived, we quietly keep the fast deliveries and drop the slow ones, and the model learns that deliveries are quicker than they really are. The fix is a maturity window: only orders old enough that almost every outcome is in, here ten days, count as labelled. Some outcomes never arrive at all. A cancelled order or a lost parcel has no delivery time, so we either exclude it and say so, or treat it as a separate outcome with its own target. And even a recorded label can be wrong. Delivery times come from driver scans, which are sometimes batched at the end of a route. Check a sample against an independent record before trusting the whole column.

Here are six rows from a raw extract, and they already hide most of what can go wrong. First, coverage. Nearly every row is from the north zone. If that is true of the whole extract, a model trained on it supports a claim about the north, not about every customer the retailer serves. Second, the first two rows are the same order. A payment retry wrote it twice. If one copy lands in training and the other in evaluation, the model is graded on an order it has already seen, so duplicates come out before any split. Third, customer c-07 owns four of the six rows. Their orders share an address, a basket style and a courier route, so they are not independent. If our claim is about new customers, every order from a customer has to sit on the same side of the split. Fourth, the timestamps mix UTC with a local offset. For a claim about future orders we sort rows in time, and sorting is only meaningful once every timestamp is in one timezone.

Cleaning data is a series of decisions about who the model is for, so each one gets written down with a count. We start from a hundred and twenty thousand raw orders. Eighteen hundred are payment-retry duplicates. Three hundred have a delivery time earlier than their checkout, which is not an unusual order but a broken pipeline, and it is worth finding out why. Nine thousand four hundred are too recent for their outcome to be known, and twenty-one hundred were cancelled and have no outcome at all. That leaves a hundred and six thousand four hundred rows, and the claim we eventually make covers only orders like those. Columns get the same treatment, with privacy in mind. The model needs to know roughly where an order is going, not the street address, so the address becomes a delivery zone. The customer id stays, but only as a grouping key. Names, emails and payment details are never needed, so they are never extracted. The less sensitive data a dataset carries, the less there is to protect and the less there is to leak.

The last idea of this chapter is a boundary on everything that follows. A predictive model answers the question: given how things currently work, what is likely to happen to this order? It does not answer: what would happen if we changed something? Here is how those get confused. Under the old policy, the express upgrade was offered mostly on far orders, and far orders are late more often. So in the historical data, express offered is a strong predictor of lateness, and a model will happily use it. Read that as a cause and you would conclude that express makes deliveries late and stop offering it. But distance drives both the offer and the lateness, and the data cannot tell us what express itself does. Predictions are valid under the policy that produced the data. Estimating the effect of an action needs a randomised experiment or causal methods, which belong to the Probability and Statistics course. And once we act on predictions, we change the data that future models learn from, which we come back to in chapter eleven.

The whole point of a model is how it behaves on orders it has never seen, so we never judge it on the orders it learned from. The modelling set is divided by role. The training portion is where everything learnable gets fitted: the coefficients, but also the scaler's means, the encoder's categories, the text vocabulary. A score on training data is a training observation; it tells you about fit, not about the future. The validation portion is where we compare candidates, a linear model against a tree, one setting against another. Because we choose based on it, its score is selection evidence, and it is optimistic about whatever won. The test portion is touched once, at the very end, to estimate the one pipeline we chose. All of this rests on an assumption: that held-out rows resemble the situation where predictions will actually be used. And there is a trap. If you look at the test score, change something, and look again, the test set has quietly become a second validation set.

There is no single correct split; there is the split that matches your claim. A random split assumes every row is an independent draw from one process that never changes, which is rarely true of orders. A stratified split is random but keeps the late class at the same rate in every part, which matters when late orders are rare. If the claim is about new customers, hold out whole customers, so that no customer's habits leak from training into evaluation. If the claim is about future orders, train on earlier weeks and evaluate on later ones, because that is how the model will be used. The plot shows the strictest case, a claim about future orders from new customers. Each dot is an order. Training uses weeks one to eight from customers one to six. Testing uses weeks nine to twelve from customers seven and eight. The grey dots, early orders from test customers and later orders from training customers, are thrown away, because putting either on the wrong side would leak one half of the claim into the other.

Before building anything ambitious, fit the baseline. Predicting the median delivery time for each zone gives a validation mean absolute error of forty-one minutes; these are illustrative numbers, but they show the pattern. A linear model on checkout features brings that to thirty-three, which is a plausible improvement. Then a third model scores six minutes. That is not a breakthrough. Delivery times vary for reasons nobody can know at checkout, traffic, weather, a customer who is not home, so a six-minute error is a symptom that the model can see something it should not. The audit on the right asks one question of every feature: was it known at the checkout click? Distance and the promise were. The courier identifier is assigned at dispatch, and the scan count accumulates while the parcel is in transit, so both are leaks. The subtle one is a zone average computed over the whole dataset, which quietly includes future deliveries. The same average computed only from the thirty days before checkout is fine.

It is tempting to think only the model learns, but preparation steps learn too. A scaler learns a mean and a standard deviation. An encoder learns which categories exist. A text vectoriser learns a vocabulary. So the same rule applies to them: learn on training data only. Scikit-learn makes the rule visible with three verbs. Fit learns state from the training fold; here, a mean distance of ten point two kilometres and a standard deviation of five. Transform applies that stored state, unchanged, to the training rows and to the validation rows alike. Predict runs the fitted model on the transformed validation rows, and the result is validation evidence. In cross-validation, which comes later, every fold refits its own state from its own training part. The classic mistake is to fit the scaler on the whole dataset before splitting. Then the validation rows have helped shape their own transformation. For a scaler the damage is usually small; for anything that learns from the target, or from text, it can be large.

Here are five validation rows of the distance feature, two of them missing. The imputer was fitted on the training fold, where the median distance was nine kilometres, so both gaps become nine point zero, the training median, not the validation median. Next to that is a missing flag. Missingness is often informative: a distance can be missing because the address could not be geocoded, and those orders may genuinely behave differently, so we let the model see it. Simply dropping incomplete rows would be worse, because it silently changes the population our claim covers. Then the scaler, also fitted on train, with a mean of ten point two and a standard deviation of five. Four point one kilometres becomes minus one point two two; twenty-two kilometres becomes two point three six. Scaling matters for models that measure distances or penalise coefficient sizes, which we meet in chapters four and five; tree models do not care. A validation value beyond the training range is not an error, but it is a place where the model is extrapolating.

Categorical and text features need encoding, and every encoder learns a vocabulary, which raises the question of what it does with something new. One-hot encoding gives each zone seen in training its own column of ones and zeros. Now the retailer opens a west zone, and a validation order arrives from it. With handle unknown set to ignore, that order gets zeros in every zone column, which the model treats as no zone information. Without that setting, the pipeline raises an error the first time it meets the new zone, which in production means a failed prediction. Text works the same way. As a separate illustration, take short customer reviews; they are not a checkout feature, because they are written after delivery. A count vectoriser builds its vocabulary from the training reviews only. A validation review containing a word first seen there, like crushed, simply loses that word. If you build the vocabulary on all the text instead, you leak which words the held-out data uses, and the validation score becomes optimistic.

Some of the strongest features summarise the past: how often has this customer's order been late, how late does this zone usually run? They are also the easiest to leak, so every one is computed as of the prediction time. Take customer c-07 checking out on the fifteenth of March. Their order from early March was delivered on the fourth, so it counts. Their order from the ninth was placed before checkout but not delivered until the sixteenth, so at the checkout click its outcome is still unknown, and it must not count. That is label maturity again, now inside a feature. Their order from the twentieth is simply in the future. Target encoding replaces a category with the average outcome for that category, which puts the target inside a feature. The safe way is cross-fitting: split the training data into folds and compute each fold's zone rate from the other folds only. The naive version, averaging over all rows, looks almost identical, but every row's own label helped compute its feature, and the model learns to trust it too much.

Everything in this chapter comes together in one object. A column transformer sends the numeric columns through a median imputer and a scaler, and the zone column through a one-hot encoder that ignores new values. A pipeline then chains that preparation with the model, here a linear regression, which is the subject of the next chapter. Now a single call to fit, on the training rows, learns every piece of state in the right order: the median, the mean and spread, the zone list, and finally the coefficients. A single call to predict on validation rows reuses all of it, and the mean absolute error that comes out is validation evidence. This is more than tidiness. Because the whole pipeline is one estimator, cross-validation and model search can refit it from scratch inside every fold, so the leaks we have been chasing cannot be written by hand. And the fitted pipeline is exactly the transformation the model was scored with, which is what we will eventually hand to engineering in chapter twelve.

A linear regression predicts a weighted sum of the features plus an intercept. On these training orders the fit says duration is about twenty-five minutes, plus four point two minutes per kilometre, plus a minute per basket item. The reading of a coefficient is precise: four point two more minutes for each extra kilometre, holding the other features fixed. The intercept is the prediction when every feature is zero, which here is an order with no distance and no items, outside anything we observe, so it is a fitting constant rather than a fact. Coefficients carry units, so a large coefficient on a feature measured in kilometres and a small one on a feature measured in metres say nothing about importance. Now add road distance, which is almost a copy of straight-line distance. Fit A puts all the weight on distance; fit B splits it between the two. Their predictions and validation error are identical. The design matrix still has full rank, because the columns are not exact copies, but they are far from independent, and the individual coefficients are no longer trustworthy as effects.

Here are six validation orders with their actual and predicted durations. The residual is actual minus predicted, so a positive residual means the order took longer than we said. Mean absolute error averages the sizes of the residuals: ten point three minutes, the typical miss. Root mean squared error squares them first, averages, and takes the square root: seventeen minutes. The difference comes almost entirely from one order that took forty minutes longer than predicted. Squaring makes large misses count far more, which is right if a long delay is much worse than two short ones, and wrong if it just reflects one strange order. The choice also changes what a model learns: minimising squared error targets the mean duration, minimising absolute error targets the median. A metric only means something next to a baseline. Predicting the median for every order gives an MAE of nineteen point five on the same rows, so the model removes about half the error, a skill of zero point four seven. And because we used these rows to compare candidates, these numbers are validation evidence, not a final result.

A linear model only has to be linear in its coefficients, not in its inputs. If we add distance squared and distance cubed as extra columns, the same linear machinery fits a curve, and that lets durations grow faster on long routes. An interaction, distance times a rush-hour flag, lets the slope itself change at busy times. Bins replace distance with bands, each with its own level. All of these are features we design, and they are fitted inside the pipeline like any other transformation. The danger is at the edges. Our training orders cover one to twenty kilometres, and inside that range the cubic fit follows the points closely. Beyond twenty kilometres there is no data at all, and the curve does whatever its basis dictates; here the cubic term makes a thirty-kilometre prediction shoot upward. That number is a property of the polynomial, not of deliveries. A linear model reports no extra uncertainty out there, so the pipeline has to notice for it: record the training range and flag inputs that fall outside it.

For late-delivery risk we need a probability, not a number of minutes. Logistic regression starts exactly like linear regression, a weighted sum of features plus an intercept, which we call the score. It then passes the score through the sigmoid function, which squashes any number into the range zero to one. A score of zero becomes a probability of one half; large positive scores approach one, large negative scores approach zero. With more than two outcomes, say early, on time and late, softmax plays the same role, turning one score per class into probabilities that add up to one. The model is fitted by minimising log loss: for each order, minus the log of the probability the model gave to what actually happened. Saying nought point nine for an order that was late costs zero point one one. Saying nought point one for an order that was late costs two point three, twenty times more. That steep penalty on confident mistakes is the point. It rewards probabilities that mean what they say, which matters later when decisions depend on them.

A classifier's output passes through several stages, and it helps to keep them apart. The model computes a score, here one point four. The sigmoid turns it into a probability, nought point eight. A threshold, here one half, turns the probability into a label, late. And the label drives a decision, offering express shipping. Do that for a thousand validation orders and count what happened. Of the hundred and fifty orders that were actually late, ninety were flagged and sixty were missed. Of the eight hundred and fifty on-time orders, seventy were flagged anyway. Precision asks, of the orders we flagged, how many were late: ninety out of a hundred and sixty, nought point five six. Recall asks, of the late orders, how many did we flag: ninety out of a hundred and fifty, nought point six. Accuracy looks impressive at nought point eight seven, until you notice that calling every single order on time scores nought point eight five. With a rare class, accuracy hides almost everything. What matters is the cost of each cell, and those costs come from the decision.

A threshold picks one point; a curve shows every point the ranking allows. Sweep the threshold from high to low and record, at each step, recall and the false-positive rate: that is the ROC curve. The area under it, about nought point eight seven here, has a clean meaning: the probability that a randomly chosen late order gets a higher score than a randomly chosen on-time one. The precision-recall curve plots the same sweep differently, precision against recall. Its reference line is not the diagonal but the base rate: a random ranking has precision nought point one five everywhere, because fifteen percent of orders are late. When positives are rare, the PR curve is the more revealing one, because the ROC curve's horizontal axis divides false alarms by eight hundred and fifty on-time orders and makes them look cheap. The marked point on both curves is the threshold of one half from the confusion matrix. With more than two classes, metrics must be averaged, and macro, micro and weighted averages answer different questions, so a reported score always says which one it is.

Ranking and probability are different properties, and a model can be good at one and poor at the other. Models A and B here put the orders in exactly the same order, so their ROC AUC is identical, nought point eight seven. But model B's probabilities are stretched upward: on average it says twenty-seven percent of orders will be late, when the real rate is fifteen. AUC is blind to that, because it only looks at order. Log loss sees it, and so does the Brier score, which is simply the mean squared difference between the predicted probability and the outcome. If all you do is rank orders and inspect the top hundred, model B is fine. If you multiply the probability by a cost to decide whether to pay for express shipping, model B will overspend, and you should judge it by a probability metric. Chapter seven returns to fixing this, with calibration. Outputs also differ in structure. Multiclass means exactly one outcome per order, early, on time or late, and the probabilities sum to one. Multilabel means several outcomes can hold together, late and damaged, each with its own probability.

Late orders are fifteen percent of the data, which is mild imbalance, but enough that an unweighted model can achieve good-looking scores while largely ignoring them. There are three standard responses. Class weights make each late order count more in the training loss; balanced weights make the two classes contribute equally. Resampling changes the training rows themselves, duplicating late orders or dropping some on-time ones. And often the simplest choice is to keep the model as it is and move the decision threshold. Whatever you do happens inside the training fold. The validation fold keeps the natural fifteen percent rate, because that is the world the model will face; resampling validation data would report performance on a population that does not exist. The table shows the trade on our validation orders. Balanced weights catch more late orders, recall rising from nought point six to nought point seven eight, at the price of more false alarms, precision falling to nought point three eight. They also inflate the probabilities: the model now averages thirty-one percent late. If those probabilities feed a cost calculation, they must be recalibrated, which is chapter seven.

Fitting a model means minimising its average loss on the training rows, which is called the empirical risk. But the training rows are only a sample, and what we actually care about is the loss on orders the model has not seen. The gap between those two is the whole subject of this chapter. Capacity is the range of shapes a model family can represent. A straight line has little; a degree-twelve polynomial has a lot. The plot shows what happens as we raise the polynomial degree on the same delivery data. Training error falls every single time, down to fifteen at degree twelve, because a more flexible curve can always pass closer to the training points. Validation error falls at first, reaches its lowest at degree four, and then climbs steeply. Past that point the extra flexibility is spent fitting the noise in this particular sample. So a low training error is a training observation and tells you almost nothing about quality. We control capacity in two ways: by choosing the model family, and by adding a penalty inside it, which comes next.

Regularisation changes what training minimises. Instead of the loss alone, it minimises the loss plus a penalty on the size of the coefficients, scaled by a strength alpha. Ridge regression penalises the sum of squared coefficients. The left plot shows its effect as alpha grows: every coefficient shrinks smoothly toward zero, but none ever gets there. Lasso penalises the sum of absolute values, and that small change has a big consequence: as alpha grows, coefficients hit zero one after another and stay there, so lasso also selects features. Elastic net mixes the two, with a parameter setting the share of each. Two rules make penalties work. First, alpha is a setting we choose on validation data; training error always prefers alpha equal to zero, because the penalty can only make training fit worse. Second, scale the features first. The penalty treats every coefficient alike, so if distance is in kilometres and basket size in items, one alpha punishes them unevenly. That is why the scaler goes inside the pipeline, ahead of the model, and gets refitted in every fold.

Lasso's feature selection is attractive, but it has a weakness with correlated features. Road distance and straight-line distance correlate at nought point nine eight; they carry almost the same information. Fit lasso on five bootstrap resamples of the same training fold, and look at which one it keeps. Twice it keeps straight-line distance and zeroes road distance. Twice it does the opposite. Once it keeps both at about half weight. The predictions in all five cases are nearly identical; what changes is which feature appears to matter. If you reported the first fit, you would say road distance is irrelevant. If you reported the second, you would say the same about straight-line distance. Ridge behaves differently: it splits the weight roughly evenly, about two each, every time. So a zero lasso coefficient means only that the feature was not needed given the others in this sample, not that it is irrelevant. Before reporting selected features, check how stable the selection is across resamples. Elastic net tends to keep correlated groups together, and often the cleanest fix is to combine the twins into one feature.

Many models, logistic regression and the lasso among them, are fitted by an iterative optimiser that takes repeated steps downhill on the training loss. The mathematics of those steps belongs to the Calculus and Optimisation course; here we need only the diagnostic reading. The plot shows the training loss for three step sizes on the same problem. With a step that is too small, the loss is still falling when the iteration limit arrives: the optimiser stopped, but it did not converge, and the coefficients you get are not the minimum the settings describe. With a step that is too large, the loss bounces back and forth and never settles. With a sensible step, the loss falls quickly and flattens, and more iterations change nothing. In practice, take convergence warnings seriously and compare the number of iterations used with the maximum allowed. Unscaled features make the loss surface long and narrow, which slows solvers down; scaling helps them converge. And keep two questions apart: a perfectly optimised training objective can still generalise badly, which is the problem regularisation addresses, not the optimiser.

Some models are trained in many passes, an epoch at a time, gradient-boosted trees and neural networks among them, and for those the number of passes is itself a capacity setting. The longer training runs, the more closely the model fits the training rows. The plot shows the familiar shape. Training loss falls with every epoch. Loss on held-out data falls at first, reaches its minimum around epoch twelve, and then rises as the model starts fitting noise. Early stopping watches that held-out loss, keeps the weights from the best epoch, and stops. The important detail is which held-out data it watches. It should be an inner split, around ten percent, carved out of the training fold. The validation fold that we use to compare candidates must stay untouched. If the same validation rows both choose the stopping epoch and then score the model, they have been used twice, and the score is optimistic. Scikit-learn's estimators that support early stopping do exactly this inner split, controlled by a validation fraction and a patience setting.

A learning curve answers a practical question: would more data help? Take the same pipeline, train it on growing slices of the training data, and at each size record both the training error and the validation error. The left plot is the high-bias shape. With little data the model fits its few training rows imperfectly, and as data grows the two curves meet, but they meet at a high error. The model is too simple for the problem, and more orders will not fix that; it needs more capacity, better features, or a smaller penalty. The right plot is the high-variance shape. Training error is very low, validation error is much higher, and the gap narrows steadily as data grows. Here more data genuinely helps, and so would a stronger penalty or a simpler model. If both curves are low and the model still disappoints in use, the problem is often not the model at all, so audit the labels and the slices of data where it fails. Each point on these curves comes from refitting the whole pipeline, and each is validation evidence.

Capacity is not free. A degree-eight polynomial with ridge does score best on validation, but only by a tenth of a minute over the cubic, and to get that tenth it takes fourteen times as long to fit, eight times as long to predict a thousand orders, and thirty-four times the memory. Whether that is worth it depends on the decision, but a tenth of a minute is smaller than the variation you would see between folds, so the honest reading is that the two are tied and the simpler one is cheaper. For a comparison like this to mean anything, the candidates must have had the same chance. They are scored on the same folds, so that one did not get easier rows. They get the same tuning budget, because a model tried with twenty settings will usually beat one tried with two, regardless of which family is better. Timings are compared on one machine, since they are relative rather than absolute. And the table should report the spread across folds, not a single number that may come from one lucky split. Chapter seven builds this into a full selection workflow.

Nearest neighbours is the most literal learning method there is. It does not fit coefficients at all; it keeps the training orders and, when a new order arrives, finds the ones most similar to it. Here each order is a point in two scaled features, and the query is the order we want to predict. We measure its distance to every training order and take the five closest, the ones inside the dashed circle. Three of them were late, two were on time, so the majority vote says late. For regression, the prediction is simply the average of their delivery times, sixty-two minutes. Notice what the classification output really is. Three out of five is a vote fraction. It is tempting to read it as a sixty percent probability, but nothing has checked that orders with this vote are late sixty percent of the time, and with five neighbours only six values are even possible. And notice where the cost sits. Fitting is just storing the data, which is instant; every prediction has to search the training set, which is where k-NN becomes expensive.

k-NN has two decisions that actually matter: how many neighbours to use, and what distance means. With k equal to one, each training order is its own nearest neighbour, so training error is zero, and validation error is high because every prediction copies a single noisy order. As k grows, predictions average over more orders and become smoother. Push k far enough and every prediction approaches the overall average, losing all local detail. On our validation data the error is lowest around ten neighbours, and like any setting, k is chosen on validation inside each fold. Distance is the subtler choice. If basket value is measured in pounds and distance in kilometres, a ten-pound difference outweighs a ten-kilometre one, and neighbours are chosen almost entirely by basket value; scaling fixes that. Irrelevant features are worse than useless, because each one adds noise to every distance. And in many dimensions a strange thing happens: the nearest and farthest training points end up almost equally far away, so being the nearest says very little. k-NN works best with a handful of meaningful, scaled features.

Naive Bayes takes a different route. Instead of drawing a boundary directly, it models how each class generates its features, and then uses Bayes' rule to reverse the direction. As an illustration we use short review texts, with two classes: reviews complaining about lateness, and the rest. Forty percent of training reviews are complaints, which is the prior. From word counts we estimate how likely each word is within each class. Then comes the naive assumption: given the class, words occur independently, so the likelihood of a whole review is the product of its word likelihoods. For the review late again, the complaint class gets nought point four times nought point five nine six times nought point two five; the other class gets a much smaller product. Normalising the two gives a ninety-four percent probability of a complaint. Smoothing adds one to every count, so a word never seen in a class does not force that class's probability to exactly zero. The independence assumption is plainly false, late and again go together, so the probabilities come out overconfident. The ranking, though, is often good, which is why naive Bayes remains a strong, cheap baseline for text.

Linear and quadratic discriminant analysis are also generative: they model each class as a Gaussian cloud and classify a point by which cloud makes it most likely. The only difference is what they assume about the clouds' shapes. LDA assumes every class shares one covariance, the same spread and tilt, just shifted to a different centre. Under that assumption the boundary between classes is always a straight line. QDA lets each class have its own covariance, and then the boundary can curve. In this example class A is tight and round while class B is wide, so QDA's boundary bends around A, while LDA has to settle for a line. QDA is not simply better. Each class now needs its own covariance matrix, and with twenty features that roughly doubles the number of parameters. With few rows in a class, those estimates become noisy, and in the extreme they collapse. LDA is more biased but steadier. Regularised covariance estimates sit between the two. And both rest on the classes being roughly Gaussian; when they are not, the boundary may still work, but the probabilities should not be trusted.

A support-vector machine asks a geometric question: of all the lines that separate the classes, which leaves the widest street between them? The decision function is again a weighted sum, w dot x plus b. The boundary is where it equals zero, and the edges of the street are where it equals plus and minus one. Making w smaller widens the street. The striking property is that only a few training points matter: those on the edge of the street or inside it, the support vectors, here four of them. Every other point could move, as long as it stays outside the street, and the boundary would not change. Real data is rarely perfectly separable, so the margin is soft. The hinge loss charges nothing for a point safely outside its margin and grows linearly as a point intrudes. The setting C prices those intrusions. Small C tolerates violations and keeps a wide margin with many support vectors; large C chases every training point and narrows the street. Like any capacity setting it is tuned on validation. And the output is a margin score, a distance from the boundary, not a probability.

Some classes cannot be split by any straight line. Here one class sits in the middle and the other surrounds it in a ring. The kernel trick handles this without changing the support-vector machinery at all. A kernel is a similarity function between two points. The radial basis function kernel, the usual default, gives two points a similarity near one when they are close and near zero when they are far apart, with a parameter gamma setting how quickly it falls off. With a kernel, the SVM's prediction becomes a weighted sum of similarities to its support vectors, and that is enough to draw the circular boundary in the plot. Mathematically it is equivalent to a linear boundary in an enormous feature space, but that space is never built. Gamma controls flexibility. With tiny gamma every point reaches far and the boundary is nearly a line; with huge gamma every point only influences its immediate surroundings and the boundary breaks into islands. Gamma and C interact, so they are tuned together, on validation, and because similarity is a distance, the features must be scaled. Training cost grows fast with the number of rows.

Support-vector regression carries the margin idea over to numeric targets. Instead of a street between classes, it fits a tube around the prediction, with a half-width called epsilon. Any order whose actual duration falls inside the tube costs nothing at all. Orders outside the tube pay a loss that grows linearly with how far outside they are, and those orders are the support vectors, five of eighteen in this plot. Epsilon is measured in the target's own units, so a six-minute tube says that errors under six minutes are not worth chasing. That is a statement about the decision, and it can be chosen deliberately rather than just tuned. With a kernel the line becomes a curve, exactly as in classification. The second half of this section is about what each model must keep in order to predict. A linear model keeps one coefficient per feature, which is cheap at any scale. k-NN keeps every training row and searches them for every prediction. Kernel SVMs and SVR keep their support vectors, which can be a large share of the data. Those memory and latency costs belong in the model comparison, not in an afterthought.

Having seen several families, the useful question is not which one is best, because none is in general, but which assumption fits this problem at a cost we can afford. k-NN assumes that nearby orders behave alike. Naive Bayes assumes features are independent within a class. LDA and QDA assume each class is a Gaussian cloud. SVMs assume a margin exists, possibly after a kernel. Several of them need scaled features: anything built on distances or penalties does, the generative models mostly do not. Their prediction costs differ by orders of magnitude, from a handful of multiplications to a search through the whole training set. And their native outputs mean different things. A k-NN vote fraction and an SVM margin score are rankings, not probabilities. Naive Bayes produces probabilities, but its false independence pushes them toward zero and one. Logistic regression and LDA aim at probabilities directly, and even they should be checked. So when these families are compared, it is on identical splits, with the metric the decision actually needs, and if probabilities feed a cost, they are calibrated first, which is chapter seven.

A decision tree predicts by asking a sequence of yes-or-no questions about the features. Training chooses each question greedily, to make the resulting groups as pure as possible. Purity is measured by an impurity score; for classification the usual one is Gini. Our hundred training orders contain thirty late ones, so the root's Gini is one minus nought point three squared minus nought point seven squared, which is nought point four two. Now try the question: is the distance at most eight kilometres? Sixty orders go left with only six late, Gini nought point one eight; forty go right with twenty-four late, Gini nought point four eight. Weighting by group size gives nought point three, a reduction of nought point one two. Splitting on rush hour instead only reduces impurity by nought point zero two, so distance becomes the root. The same search repeats inside each group: the far orders split again on rush hour. Each leaf predicts its own late fraction, so a far order at rush hour gets eighty percent. Regression trees work the same way with squared error, predicting leaf means. And because only the order of values matters, trees need no scaling.

Without limits a tree keeps splitting until every leaf is pure, and at that point it has memorised the training orders. The plot shows the familiar pattern with depth as capacity: training loss falls toward zero, validation loss is lowest around depth four and then rises. There are several ways to hold a tree back. Maximum depth caps the number of questions on any path. A minimum leaf size refuses to create leaves too small to estimate a rate reliably. Cost-complexity pruning grows the full tree and then removes branches whose improvement does not justify their size, controlled by one parameter. All of these are chosen on validation. The other weakness of trees is instability. Fit the same depth-four tree on two bootstrap resamples of the same training fold, and the first split changes: one tree splits on straight-line distance, the other on road distance, then they diverge further. Yet their validation scores are almost identical. The accuracy is stable; the structure is not. So one tree's shape should never be read as the truth about the data. And that very instability is what ensembles turn into an advantage.

A single deep tree has low bias and high variance: it fits the training data closely, and a slightly different sample gives a very different tree. Averaging is the classic cure for variance, but only if the things being averaged are not all making the same mistakes. A random forest builds that diversity in two ways. Each tree trains on a bootstrap resample of the training fold, which is called bagging. And at every split, each tree may only consider a random subset of the features, so even a dominant feature like distance is sometimes unavailable, and the trees are forced to differ. The forest predicts the average of its trees. The effect shows up clearly across random seeds. One deep tree averages twelve point four minutes of error, but that number moves by nearly two minutes from seed to seed. A five-hundred-tree forest scores nine point one, with a spread of only a fifth of a minute. Adding more trees does not cause overfitting; it only costs time and memory. And the orders left out of each tree's resample provide a free out-of-bag estimate, which comes with a caveat at the end of this chapter.

Boosting builds an ensemble in a completely different way. Instead of independent trees averaged at the end, it adds trees one at a time, and each new tree is fitted to whatever the current ensemble still gets wrong. Here is one round on five training orders. We start from the simplest possible model, a constant: the mean duration, sixty-four minutes. The residuals are what that misses: the three short orders are over-predicted by twenty-four, fourteen and four minutes, the two long orders are under-predicted by eleven and thirty-one. Now fit a tiny tree, a single split on distance, to those residuals. It predicts minus fourteen for short orders and plus twenty-one for long ones. We add half of that tree's output, a learning rate of nought point five, to the constant. The training mean squared error drops from three hundred and seventy-four to a hundred and fifty-three point five, and the next tree is fitted to the new, smaller residuals. For squared error, the residual is exactly the negative gradient of the loss, which is how boosting generalises to log loss and others. Forests attack variance; boosting attacks bias, which is why boosting can overfit if it runs too long.

Gradient boosting has three settings that interact so strongly they are best thought of as one budget: the learning rate, the number of rounds, and the size of each tree. The plot shows held-out loss against the number of rounds for two learning rates. With a learning rate of nought point three, the loss drops fast, reaches its best around round eighty, and then creeps back up as later trees start fitting noise. With nought point zero five, each step is small, so it takes hundreds of rounds to get anywhere, but it ends up lower and stays there longer. That pattern is typical: smaller steps tend to generalise better, at the price of more computation. Tree size sets how much each round can learn; small trees with a modest number of leaves are the norm. The practical recipe is to fix a small learning rate, set the maximum number of rounds generously as an upper bound, and let early stopping pick the actual number. As in chapter four, the stopping split comes from inside the training fold, so the validation fold stays clean for comparing the learning rate and tree size.

Different model families make different mistakes. A linear model captures smooth trends, a forest picks up interactions, k-NN catches local patterns, boosting chases residual structure. Combining them can beat each one, but only to the extent that their errors differ. The simplest combination is to average their predictions, or for classes to vote, with equal weights. Stacking goes further: a second-level model, the meta-model, learns how much weight each base model deserves. The trap is in what the meta-model learns from. If the base models predict the same orders they were trained on, a flexible model like the forest will look nearly perfect on those orders, and the meta-model will learn to trust it far too much. So the inputs to the meta-model must be out-of-fold predictions: split the training data into five folds, fit each base model on four of them, and predict the fifth. The table shows those columns: every number is a prediction for an order that particular model never saw. The meta-model, here a ridge regression, is then fitted on those honest predictions. Scikit-learn's stacking estimators do this internally with their cv setting.

Every tree ensemble can report a feature importance at no extra cost, by adding up how much each feature reduced impurity across all its splits. That number is computed on the training data, and it has a known bias toward features with many possible split points. The table makes the point with a column that is pure noise: a random hash of the order identifier. Because it takes thousands of distinct values, the trees find plenty of splits on it that happen to fit the training data, and its impurity importance comes out at nought point two one, more than rush hour. Permutation importance asks a different question on validation data: if we shuffle this column, how much worse do predictions get? For the hash, not at all. Chapter eleven develops permutation importance properly. Remember too that correlated features split their importance between them, under either measure. Trees also differ in what inputs they accept. Histogram-based boosting handles missing values natively by learning which branch they should follow, and can treat declared categorical columns natively. Other tree implementations vary by library and version, so check the documentation of the version you run rather than assuming.

By the end of this chapter the candidates are a logistic baseline, a single shallow tree, a random forest and a gradient-boosted model, all scored on the same grouped-temporal validation folds. The ensembles win on log loss, as they usually do, so the remaining questions are about evidence, probabilities and cost. First, evidence. The forest's out-of-bag estimate says nought point two seven, noticeably better than the nought point three three the validation folds report. The difference is not a mystery: out-of-bag rows are random rows, so the same customer's orders and later orders sit on both sides, which is exactly what our future-order claim forbids. Out-of-bag is convenient, but here it is optimistic, and the validation folds are the evidence. Second, probabilities. Averaging many trees tends to squeeze a forest's probabilities toward the middle, so they need checking before they feed a cost decision; boosting with log loss is often closer, but is checked too. Third, cost. The forest takes a hundred and eighty megabytes and forty-five milliseconds per thousand orders; boosting two megabytes and six. Here the more accurate model is also the cheaper one.

A single validation split wastes data and gives a noisy score, so model selection normally uses cross-validation: the development data, meaning everything except the locked test set, is split into several folds, and each fold takes a turn as validation while the others train. Two rules make it valid. First, the folds must follow the claim. For future orders, time-series splits always train on the past and validate on the future; for new customers, group folds keep each customer's orders together. Second, the search is over whole pipelines. The imputation strategy is a choice just like the learning rate, and searching them jointly, inside a pipeline, means every candidate is refitted from scratch inside every fold, with no preparation state leaking across. Here eight candidates are scored on five folds, forty pipeline fits in all. The best averages nought point three one zero, but two others are within one fold standard deviation of it. And the winning mean is selection evidence, not an estimate of future performance: when you pick the best of eight noisy scores, the one you pick is likely to have been lucky.

Every extra candidate you try is another chance for one of them to win by luck, so a trustworthy search is declared before it runs. Fix a budget, a number of trials per model family, so that a heavily tuned favourite is not compared against an untuned rival. If features are selected automatically, that selection is a fitted step like any other: it lives inside the pipeline and is redone in every fold, because selecting features on all the development data and then cross-validating leaks the selection into the scores. And log every trial, not just the winner, so that anyone reading the result knows how many shots were taken. Ablation is the complementary tool for understanding what the chosen pipeline relies on. Remove one feature group at a time, refit the whole pipeline on the same folds, and record the change. Removing rush hour costs one point two minutes of error, and the as-of history features nought point nine; both clearly carry signal. Removing zone or basket size changes the error by less than fold-to-fold noise. Note what ablation measures: how much this model uses a group, not whether the group causes delays.

Cross-validated search gives us a winner and a score, but that score was used to choose the winner, so it is biased upward. To estimate how well the whole procedure generalises, including the act of searching, the search itself has to be evaluated on data it never saw. That is nested cross-validation. The outer loop splits the development data into folds. For each outer fold, a complete inner cross-validated search runs on the outer training part only and picks its settings. Those chosen settings are then refitted and scored on the outer held-out part. Different outer folds may pick slightly different settings, and that is fine: we are evaluating the procedure, not one configuration. The table shows the gap. The inner best scores average nought point three zero, but the outer scores average nought point three three, with a spread of about nought point zero two. That difference is the optimism of selection. Notice that the final test set is still locked; nested evaluation happens entirely within the development data. Nested CV is expensive, and when you cannot afford it, at least never report the inner best as your estimate.

Two diagnostic habits separate a careful evaluation from a single number. The first concerns comparisons. Candidates A and B are scored on the same five folds, so we can compare them fold by fold: A is better on four of the five, by about a sixth of a minute on average. That pairing is far more informative than comparing two means. But be careful about what the spread of fold scores means. The folds share most of their training rows, so the five scores are not independent measurements, and treating their standard deviation as a confidence interval overstates how sure we are. The second habit is to look inside the error. The overall validation error is eight point seven minutes, but that average hides slices where the model does much worse: the east zone at fourteen point two, new customers at eleven and a half, rush hour at nearly eleven. Those slices tell you where to improve features, and where the model should not be trusted. Large baskets look worst of all, but on only sixty orders, so that estimate is weak. Every slice is reported with its count.

Chapter three showed that ranking and probability quality are different things. Calibration is about the second. A model is calibrated if its probabilities mean what they say: among all the orders it scores at thirty percent, about thirty percent are actually late. The reliability diagram checks this directly. Bin held-out predictions by their predicted probability, and for each bin plot the mean prediction against the fraction that were actually late. A calibrated model sits on the diagonal. Our raw forest does not. Its predictions are squeezed toward the middle: orders it scores at fifteen percent are late only six percent of the time, and orders it scores at sixty-five percent are late eighty-eight percent of the time. Calibration fits a monotone mapping from raw scores to corrected probabilities, isotonic or sigmoid. Because the mapping is monotone, the ranking and the AUC do not change. The calibrator learns from labels, so it must be fitted on rows the model did not train on, either a separate split or cross-validation, which is what scikit-learn's calibrated classifier does. And the final judgement of the calibrated model happens on the test set, once.

The threshold is where a model's probabilities become actions, and the default of one half is almost never the right choice. The right choice comes from the costs of the two mistakes. Suppose a late order we fail to flag costs eight pounds in vouchers and lost goodwill, while an unnecessary express offer costs three pounds. Then for a thousand validation orders, the expected cost at any threshold is eight times the misses plus three times the false alarms, and we can read it off the validation counts. The curve is lowest at a threshold of nought point three, six hundred and twenty-two pounds, against six hundred and ninety at the default. That is close to what theory predicts: with calibrated probabilities, flag an order when its probability exceeds three over three plus eight, about nought point two seven. Sometimes the constraint is capacity rather than cost. If the courier can only take two hundred express orders per thousand, we flag the top two hundred by score, which corresponds to about nought point four, and accept a higher cost. Either way, the threshold, the costs and the capacity are fixed on validation, before the test set is opened.

A predicted duration of forty-five minutes says nothing about how sure the model is. Quantile models make the uncertainty visible. Instead of predicting the mean, a model can be trained with quantile loss to predict a chosen percentile. Fit one for the tenth percentile and one for the ninetieth, and together they give a nominal eighty percent interval for each order. In the plot the band widens on long routes, where delivery times genuinely vary more. For the customer-facing promise, the ninetieth percentile is often the more useful number than the median. Now the honest part. The band claims eighty percent coverage, so check it on held-out data. Overall, seventy-eight percent of validation orders fall inside, close to nominal. But at rush hour it is seventy-one percent, and in the newly opened west zone only sixty-one. Nominal coverage is a target the method aims at, not a guarantee; methods with formal guarantees exist but are beyond this course. Where the interval is too wide to be useful, or coverage is known to be weak, the system can abstain: fall back to a fixed rule, or send the case to a person.

Model selection ends with a short, strict sequence. Everything is chosen on the development data: the pipeline and its settings by cross-validation within a declared budget, the calibrator on its own split, the threshold by cost or capacity. Then the chosen pipeline is refitted on all of the development data, because more data usually helps and nothing remains to be chosen. Then, and only then, the locked test set is opened and the refitted pipeline is scored on it once: a log loss of nought point three two. If anything is changed after seeing that number, the test set has become validation data and no longer provides a final estimate. The result is written down as a record in which every number says what kind of evidence it is. The cross-validated score of nought point three one is selection evidence. The nested estimate of nought point three three estimates the whole procedure. The test score of nought point three two is the final result, though still a single sample with its own noise. Beside them sit the calibration method, the threshold and its justification, and the known limits, such as weak interval coverage in new zones.

Unsupervised learning begins with a different question about the inputs: can we describe them with fewer numbers? Every answer to that question decides what is worth preserving, and different methods preserve different things. There are two broad routes. Selection keeps a subset of the original columns, so the result is still readable: distance is still distance, in kilometres. Extraction builds new columns, each one a weighted combination of all the originals, which can be more compact but no longer has a plain meaning. The table lists the methods in this chapter by their objective. Lasso selects columns by how much they help predict the target, and it is the only one here that looks at the target at all. A variance threshold drops near-constant columns. PCA keeps as much variance as possible. Truncated SVD reconstructs sparse data. NMF finds additive parts with no negative values. And t-SNE and UMAP preserve local neighbourhoods to draw a picture. The point to carry through the chapter is that none of the unsupervised objectives promises to keep what predicts delivery time. Whether a reduction helps a task is something we measure.

Principal component analysis finds the directions along which the data varies most. The plot shows two scaled features that move together, straight-line distance and road distance. The first step is to centre each feature by subtracting its training mean, so that the cloud sits around the origin. Then the singular value decomposition of the centred matrix gives a set of orthogonal directions, ordered by how much variance lies along each. The first principal component points along the shared trend of the two distances; almost all the variation is there. The second is at right angles to it and carries what little is left, the detour that makes road distance differ from a straight line. A row's score on a component is its projection onto that direction, and keeping k components means keeping the first k score columns as the new features. Two cautions. A component and its negative are equally valid, so the sign of an arrow means nothing. And the derivation of why the SVD gives these directions belongs to the Linear Algebra course; here we only need to use it correctly.

Each principal component explains a share of the total variance in the training data, and the curve shows how those shares add up. The first component keeps forty-six percent, the first three together seventy-nine percent, and the last few components carry almost nothing. Dropping them loses little in reconstruction: if you project the data onto three components and map back, the rebuilt orders are close to the originals. But keep in mind that a small reconstruction error is not the same thing as a small loss of predictive information, which is the subject of the last section. Scaling matters even more for PCA than for distance-based models, because variance depends on units. The table shows the loadings of the first component, its weights on each feature. Unscaled, basket value measured in pounds has by far the largest numbers, so it dominates: the first component is basically basket value, with a loading of nought point nine nine. After scaling, the first component is a genuine mix of distance, road distance, item count and value. PCA on unscaled mixed units is mostly measuring the choice of units.

Text features are a different shape of data: thousands of word columns, almost all zero, and never negative. As a separate illustration, take four thousand training reviews turned into a term matrix with three thousand columns, ninety-nine percent of it zeros. Standard PCA would start by centring every column, which turns all those zeros into small non-zero numbers and destroys the sparsity that makes the matrix cheap to store and compute with. Truncated SVD skips the centring and works directly on the sparse matrix, so it is the usual choice for compressing text. Its components can have negative weights, though, which makes them hard to interpret. Non-negative matrix factorisation adds a constraint: every review is written as an additive mix of parts, and both the parts and the mixing weights must be non-negative. That constraint often makes the parts readable. Here one part is dominated by late, waiting and again, another by damaged, box and broken. NMF's fit is a local solution that depends on its starting point, so fix the initialisation and check that the parts are stable. And all of it, vocabulary included, is fitted on training reviews only.

Some reductions exist only to draw a picture. t-SNE and UMAP take many dimensions, here a summary of each customer's order history, and lay the customers out in two dimensions so that customers who are similar end up near each other. The map on the left shows three tight islands. That is useful for looking: you can spot groups, outliers, and rows whose labels seem wrong. But these methods are built to preserve local neighbourhoods, and they trade away almost everything else to do it. The distance between two islands does not mean the groups are that far apart in the original data. The size of an island does not tell you how spread out that group really is. Separated islands are a hint that structure exists, not proof that there are three real classes, and the next chapter is about testing that properly. The picture also depends on settings such as perplexity, so look at several before believing any one. And scikit-learn's t-SNE has no transform method: it cannot place a new customer on an existing map, so it is not a feature-engineering step for a model.

When a reduction feeds a predictive model, it stops being a picture and becomes a pipeline step, subject to all the rules of chapter two. The scaler, the PCA and the model sit in one pipeline and are refitted inside every fold. Fitting PCA on all the rows first would let the held-out rows shape the components, which is a leak. And the number of components is a setting like any other, chosen by the model's validation score, not by a rule of thumb. The table shows why that matters. Keeping two components, sixty-seven percent of the variance, gives a cross-validated error of eleven point four minutes. Keeping three, seventy-nine percent, gives ten point nine. Using all eight features with no reduction gives nine. The reason is the rush-hour flag. It is a binary feature with little variance, so PCA treats it as unimportant and it ends up in a late component that the cut-off throws away, yet it is one of the strongest predictors of delay. A variance threshold judges the inputs; only downstream validation judges usefulness. Here the honest conclusion is that no reduction is best.

Clustering is unsupervised: there is no delivery time or late flag to check against, only the inputs. That makes one decision dominate everything else: what counts as a group. Our data for this chapter is a customer summary taken as of a fixed date, the thirty-first of March, built only from orders delivered by then, so it obeys the same as-of rule as chapter two. Each row is a customer, with their number of orders in the last ninety days, mean basket value, share of late deliveries, and zone. Notice the customer with no recent orders at all: whether they belong in the analysis, and how their missing basket value is represented, is a decision that shapes every result. There are four broad definitions of a cluster. Centroid methods like k-means say a group is the points near a centre. Connectivity methods build groups by merging close pairs. Density methods say a group is a dense region separated from others by sparse space. Model-based methods treat groups as components of a probability mixture. Every one of them rests on a notion of distance, so scaling and the choice of features come before any algorithm.

k-means is the workhorse of clustering, and its mechanism fits in two steps. Start with k centroids, here three, placed deliberately badly so we can watch them move. Assign every customer to the nearest centroid. Then move each centroid to the mean of the customers assigned to it. Repeat. Each of those steps can only lower the inertia, the total squared distance from every customer to its own centroid, so the algorithm always settles. The trace shows it exactly, computed from the plotted points. From the poor start, inertia is ninety-four point six. After one round of assigning and updating, twenty point three. Then seven point three, then six point six, and after that nothing changes: the assignments are stable and the centroids stop moving. The dashed paths in the plot show where each centroid travelled. k-means builds in strong assumptions. It favours roughly round groups of similar size in the scaled feature space, it needs k fixed in advance, and it forces every customer into some group, even an obvious outlier. The answer also depends on where you start, which is why scikit-learn uses careful starting points and several restarts by default.

Hierarchical clustering builds a whole family of answers at once. Start with every customer as its own group. Find the two closest groups and merge them. Repeat until everything is one group. The dendrogram records the history: each join is drawn at the height where the merge happened. In this example customers one and two are merged first, at a height of nought point four, then four and five, then customer three joins the first pair, customer six joins the second, and finally the two halves merge at three point two. To get actual clusters you cut the tree horizontally. Cutting at two gives two groups, and the long vertical stretch between one point four and three point two suggests that two is a natural number of groups for these customers. The important choice is the linkage, the rule for how far apart two groups are. Single linkage uses the closest pair of points, which lets groups chain into long strings. Complete linkage uses the farthest pair, giving compact groups. Ward linkage merges whichever pair increases within-group variance least, and behaves much like k-means. All of them need pairwise distances, so the cost grows quickly with the number of customers.

DBSCAN defines a cluster by density instead of by a centre. A point is a core point if at least a minimum number of other points lie within a distance called eps. Clusters grow by linking core points that are within reach of one another, and any point that no core point reaches is labelled noise. Two things follow. Clusters can take any shape, as long as they are dense. And not every point has to belong somewhere: an isolated customer is reported as noise rather than forced into the nearest group. The number of clusters is found, not chosen in advance. The price is sensitivity to eps, and the table, computed on these two half-moons, shows how sharp it is. With eps nought point three, the neighbourhoods are too small, and the moons shatter into five pieces with ten noise points. At nought point four, both moons are recovered exactly, and the five scattered points are labelled noise. At nought point four five, the neighbourhoods bridge the gap and the two moons merge into one cluster. k-means, asked for two clusters, cuts straight across both shapes and gets only seventy-three percent of the points into the right group.

With no labels, there is no accuracy to compute, and every clustering algorithm will happily return a partition for any number of groups you ask for. So a partition has to be justified with evidence of three different kinds. The first is internal: measures computed from the geometry alone. The silhouette score compares, for each customer, the average distance to its own cluster with the distance to the nearest other cluster. On our summary it peaks at three clusters, at nought point five two. But internal scores only measure shape, and they tend to reward the shapes their own method already assumes. The second kind is stability. Refit the clustering on bootstrap resamples of the customers and ask whether the same groups come back, measured by the adjusted Rand index. Three clusters return almost unchanged, an index of nought point nine one; four clusters do not, at nought point six two, which suggests the fourth group is an artefact of this sample. The third kind is domain evidence, and it is the one that decides: can the groups be named, and would a marketing or operations team actually do something different for each? A tidy partition nobody can act on is not useful.

A Gaussian mixture model turns clustering into density estimation. It says each customer was drawn from one of several Gaussian components, each with its own weight, centre and spread, and the overall density is their weighted sum. Here, on mean basket value, one component represents small baskets around twenty-five pounds, with weight nought point six, and the other large baskets around sixty pounds, with weight nought point four. The model's answer for a customer is not a single label but a set of probabilities, called responsibilities: the share of the density at that customer's value that each component contributes. The table computes them. A customer averaging thirty pounds is ninety-eight percent small-basket. A customer at forty-five pounds is ninety-eight percent large-basket. A customer at thirty-eight sits between the two, sixty-one percent and thirty-nine percent, and the model says so, where k-means would force a hard choice. The parameters are fitted by expectation-maximisation. The E-step computes every customer's responsibilities from the current components; the M-step refits each component using those responsibilities as weights. Each round cannot lower the training likelihood, and it converges to a local optimum.

Kernel density estimation estimates a distribution without assuming any components at all. Place a small bump, here a Gaussian, on every training customer's basket value, and add them up. The only real choice is the bandwidth, the width of each bump, and the plot shows how much it matters on the same seventy customers. With a bandwidth of one and a half pounds, every customer gets a sharp spike, and the estimate is a portrait of this particular sample rather than of the population. With twenty pounds, the bumps blur into one broad hump and the two groups we know are there disappear. At five, there are two clear modes, close to the mixture from the last section. The bandwidth is chosen like any other capacity setting, on held-out data. Score the thirty held-out customers by their mean log-density under each estimate: five pounds scores best, minus four point five eight, ahead of twenty and well ahead of one and a half. Do not choose it on training likelihood, which always prefers a narrower bandwidth. And remember that a better density fit says nothing about what the modes mean; naming them is still domain work.

Two practical problems remain. The first is that k-means and EM only find a local best, a solution that no single step can improve, which is not necessarily the best one. The table, computed on our customers, runs k-means from ten random starts and lets each converge. The best reaches an inertia of six point six. Three of the ten stall in clearly worse solutions, the worst at forty-three point four, typically with two centroids sharing one group while another group is split. The remedy is simple: run several starts and keep the best, which is what the n init setting does. Mixtures have an extra failure. A component can shrink onto a single customer, its variance heading toward zero and its likelihood toward infinity, which looks like a superb fit and is meaningless. A small covariance regularisation prevents it, and the number of components is compared with a penalised criterion such as BIC, or with held-out likelihood. The second problem is new customers. k-means and mixtures can assign a new customer directly. DBSCAN and agglomerative clustering in scikit-learn have no predict method, so you refit, or train a classifier on the cluster labels.

Anomaly detection asks which orders are unusual, and that question has no answer until you say unusual compared with what. So this chapter uses a separately specified task with its own contract. The unit is one order at checkout. The reference population is checkout orders from the same zone over the previous ninety days, so a large order in a business district is compared with that district, not with the whole country. A flagged order is held for a quick data-quality check, and there is a budget of fifty reviews a day. The contract also says what a flag does not claim: it is not an accusation of fraud, and it says nothing about anyone's intent. That matters, because an unusual order can be many things. It can be rare but entirely legitimate, like forty items ordered for an office. It can be a corrupt record, thirty items with a basket value of zero, which is exactly what the check is meant to catch. Or it can reflect a change in the process, such as a newly opened zone whose ordinary orders look odd against an old reference. A detector says an order is unlike the reference; only a review says why.

There are two settings that look alike and are not. In outlier detection, the data you fit on already contains anomalies, and the question is which of these particular orders are odd. In novelty detection, the reference data is believed to be clean, and the question is whether a new order, arriving later, is unlike it. Which setting you are in depends on what the reference population contains, and that is a property of the data pipeline, not of the algorithm. Local outlier factor in scikit-learn makes the difference explicit. In its default mode it is an outlier detector: you call fit predict on a dataset and it labels the rows of that same dataset, and it has no way to score an order it was not fitted on. With novelty set to true, it becomes a novelty detector: it can score new orders, and it must not be used to label its own training rows, because each training row would count itself among its neighbours. Isolation forest and one-class SVM support both uses, but the meaning of their scores still depends on which setting you are in, so the contract should say.

Two widely used detectors embody different ideas of what unusual means. Local outlier factor compares each order's local density, how tightly packed its nearest neighbours are, with the local densities of those neighbours. A score near one means the order is about as dense as its neighbourhood; a score well above one means it sits in a sparser spot than its neighbours do. Isolation forest builds many random trees that split the data on random features at random values, and measures how many splits it takes to isolate each order. Unusual points are separated from the rest in few steps. Its score is near a half for ordinary points and closer to one for points that are easy to isolate. The table, computed from these synthetic orders, shows where the two disagree. Order A, between the everyday and bulk groups, is flagged by both: a local outlier factor of four point six three and an isolation score of nought point six four. Order B sits inside the sparse group of bulk orders. LOF scores it nought point nine six, perfectly normal for a bulk order. The isolation forest gives it nought point six, nearly as high as A, because it treats the whole sparse group as unusual. Order C is ordinary to both.

In this reference cloud, item count and basket value rise together, so the cloud is a long, tilted ellipse. Ordinary distance treats every direction alike, and that misleads. Order P is less than one unit from the centre in plain distance, but it sits off to the side, across the narrow width of the cloud, where almost no orders lie. Mahalanobis distance measures distance in units of the cloud's own spread in each direction, and it puts P at seven point six four, far outside. Order Q is twice as far from the centre in plain distance, but it lies along the long axis, where orders are common, and its Mahalanobis distance is two point seven three, inside the boundary drawn at three. An elliptic envelope is exactly this: estimate the mean and covariance, and flag orders beyond a chosen Mahalanobis radius. It assumes the reference is a single Gaussian cloud, and the estimates of mean and covariance are themselves pulled toward any outliers in the reference, which is why a robust estimator is used. A one-class SVM makes a weaker assumption, drawing a flexible kernel boundary around the reference, with a parameter nu that bounds the fraction flagged. Both need scaled features.

An anomaly detector produces a score, and the first practical job is to know which way it points. In scikit-learn, score samples is lower for more abnormal orders. Decision function shifts that score so that negative values are the ones flagged at the estimator's default threshold. And that default comes from the contamination setting, which is simply your guess at the share of anomalies; it is not something the model measured. So the threshold is better set by the decision it serves. Here the data-quality team can review fifty orders a day.
