On a validation month of orders, about four thousand a day, the curve shows how many alerts each threshold produces, and a threshold of minus nought point five five gives fifty a day. Because the team reviewed that month's alerts, we can also say how many were real data errors: thirty-one percent at that threshold. A stricter threshold raises the confirmed share, to forty-five percent at minus nought point six, but flags fewer orders and misses more errors. The useful report is both numbers together, alerts per day and the share confirmed, not a score on its own.

Two difficulties shape how anomaly detectors are evaluated. The first is labels: there are almost none. Nobody knows in advance which orders are data errors, and the only labels come from reviewing alerts. The second is that detectors react to every change in what they are compared against. The plot shows both. In week six the retailer opens a west zone, which has no ninety-day history of its own. Its perfectly ordinary orders look unusual against the existing reference, and around nine percent of them are flagged, against about one percent in the north. Nothing has gone wrong with the orders; the reference no longer covers them. Once the west zone has its own reference, in week ten, its alert rate falls to about one and a half percent. Evaluating honestly under these conditions means reviewing a random sample of alerts to estimate precision, scoring each order against its own group's reference when groups genuinely differ, and re-checking whenever the process changes. And remember the blind spot of review: only flagged orders get labelled, so errors the detector misses never show up in the numbers.

Requests to explain a model usually bundle several different questions together, and each one needs a different tool. Global questions are about the model as a whole: what does it rely on, and how do its predictions change as an input like distance changes? Local questions are about one prediction: why did this particular order get seventy-four minutes? Subgroup questions ask where, and for whom, the model is wrong, which is the subject of the second half of this chapter. And then there is a question that sounds like the others but is not: would giving this order express shipping make it arrive on time? That is a causal question about an intervention. A predictive model describes the associations in data produced under the existing policy, and, as chapter one warned, it cannot say what would happen if we acted differently. Answering that needs a randomised experiment or causal methods, which belong to other courses. So everything in this chapter explains the model, evaluated on held-out data. It tells us what the model does, which is necessary for using it responsibly, but it is not a description of how deliveries work.

Three different numbers are commonly reported as feature importance, and on our model they tell three different stories. A ridge coefficient on scaled features says how much the prediction changes per standard deviation of that feature, holding the others fixed. Even scaled, correlated twins split the credit between them: distance gets five point one and road distance four point eight, and either alone would get most of the combined weight. Correlation with the target is a marginal measure that ignores everything else. Rush hour correlates only weakly with duration overall, nought point two eight, because most orders are not at rush hour, yet it has the largest coefficient, because when it applies it matters a lot. Impurity importance from a forest is computed on training data, and as chapter six showed, it favours features with many possible split points. None of these is wrong, but each answers a narrower question than how important is this feature, and none of them is a causal effect. For the question we usually mean, what does the model rely on when it predicts new orders, there is a better tool, and it is next.

Two tools answer the global questions properly, and both are computed on held-out data. Permutation importance takes one feature column in the test set, shuffles it so it no longer lines up with its rows, and measures how much the model's error rises. If the model relied on that column, error goes up a lot. Shuffling rush hour adds three point four minutes of mean absolute error; distance two point one; the as-of history features one point eight; zone almost nothing. That measures this model's reliance on each feature, with this data; it is not the feature's value in some general sense. Partial dependence answers how a feature is used. Sweep distance from zero to twenty kilometres for every order, keeping their other features as observed, and average the predictions: that is the partial-dependence curve. Individual conditional expectation lines show the same sweep for single orders; here they run roughly parallel, so distance acts similarly for everyone. Two cautions. Sweeping creates rows that never occur, like a twenty-kilometre order in a zone only five kilometres across. And where few training orders exist, beyond fourteen kilometres here, the curve shows the model extrapolating.

An explanation is itself an estimate, and like any estimate it varies. Repeat permutation importance across twenty bootstrap refits of the model and plot the range. Rush hour is stable: its importance stays between about three and four minutes every time, so we can say with some confidence that the model relies on it. Distance and road distance are a different story. Each ranges from well under one minute to over three, because in some refits the model leans on one and in others on the other. Their individual ranking is not meaningful, but their combined importance is, so correlated features are better grouped and permuted together. Some limits remain however many times you repeat. The explanation describes the model's behaviour, not the delivery process. A feature with high importance is not a lever: the model's reliance on rush hour does not mean that changing an order's timing would change its outcome, because the data cannot separate rush hour from everything that comes with it. So report explanations as ranges, group features that move together, and always say what the explanation is of.

Fairness work starts with a plain measurement: is the model's error spread evenly, or does it fall on some groups more than others? Here is recall of late orders on the test set, by group, each with a ninety-five percent interval computed from that group's own count. In the north, with four hundred late orders, recall is nought point six four with a narrow interval. In the newly opened west zone there were only twenty-five late orders, and recall is nought point four, with an interval so wide that it overlaps almost every other group. So the right statement is that there is evidence the model catches fewer late orders in the west and among new customers, and that the size of the gap is uncertain where the counts are small. Reporting a subgroup score without its denominator hides exactly that. The useful next step is to ask where such gaps come from. Sampling: the west has few orders to learn from. Labels: the east's batched driver scans make its durations noisier. Features: new customers have no as-of history at all. And history: the old express policy shaped which orders were late in the training data.

Once uneven error is measured, the next question is what fair would mean, and here mathematics sets a hard constraint. Suppose zone A has a true late rate of twelve percent and zone B twenty-four percent. With one well-calibrated model and a single threshold, zone B gets flagged more often, twenty-nine percent of orders against fourteen, simply because more of its orders really are at risk. If we instead insist on equal flag rates, twenty percent in both, recall moves apart: three quarters of zone A's late orders are caught, but only fifty-five percent of zone B's. When base rates differ, equal flag rates, equal recall and equal calibration cannot all hold together. Choosing among them is a policy decision about who bears which errors, and it belongs with the people accountable for the service, not with a library default. Three more points sit around the numbers. Zone may act as a proxy for characteristics such as income or ethnicity, even though none is in the data. Measuring group gaps may require sensitive data, which needs privacy care. And no metric in this chapter certifies a system as fair or legally compliant.

A deployed model does not just observe the world; it changes it. When the late-risk model flags an order, the retailer upgrades it to express, and most of those orders then arrive on time. Their labels, collected a week later, say on time: only nine percent of flagged, upgraded orders were late. Retrain naively on those labels and the next model learns that orders which look high-risk are actually fine, stops flagging them, and the late deliveries return. The fix is to keep one honest measurement. Hold back a small random share of flagged orders, here five percent, that receive no intervention. Their late rate, forty-one percent, is what the risk really is without express shipping. The difference between the two groups is the effect of the intervention, and because the holdout was random, it is an experiment rather than a prediction, which is exactly the causal evidence chapter one said a predictive model cannot provide. People in the loop need the same care. Overrides should be logged with a reason, and if reviewers agree with the model almost every time, audit those cases: that can be automation bias rather than agreement.

The final step of responsible use is documentation, written so that someone who was not in the room can tell what the model is for and where it stops. A model card does this in a page. It states the intended use: offering express shipping when the late-risk probability exceeds nought point three. Just as important, it states what the model is not for: it was not built or evaluated for pricing, for scoring customers, or for reviewing couriers, and using it there would be using it outside its evidence. It records the data it was trained on and the claim that evidence supports, future orders, with new customers checked separately. It gives the final test result, labelled as a single final test, and the subgroup results with their denominators, including the weak recall in the new west zone. It lists known limits: new zones, the feedback loop from interventions, and noisy labels from batched scans. And it names an owner and a review schedule. The card is versioned with the model and reviewed whenever the data, the policy, or the population changes, because a card that describes last year's model is worse than none.

The capstone pulls the course together on the late-risk task, and it begins exactly where chapter one did, with the contract, now written down as a manifest that pins every choice before any model is compared. The unit is one order. The target is whether it is delivered after the promise shown at checkout, and the prediction time is the checkout click, so every feature must exist by then. The claim is about future orders, with new customers checked as a separate question. The data is a named snapshot taken on the thirty-first of March: a hundred and six thousand four hundred orders after the exclusions logged in chapter one. The split is temporal: development data runs to January, and February and March form a locked test set. The baseline is the zone's base late rate, with a log loss of nought point four one, scored exactly the same way as every candidate will be. And the metrics are named now: log loss, cost at the chosen threshold, and subgroup recall. Pinning all of this first is what makes everything after it comparable, and the split is stored as code that rebuilds it, not as a saved list of row identifiers.

The comparison itself is a single recorded run that someone else could repeat. One configuration file names the data snapshot by its hash, the split, the random seed, the tuning budget, the library versions and the metric. Every candidate is a whole pipeline, preparation included, refitted from scratch inside every fold of the same time-series split, with the same budget of twenty trials per family, and every trial is logged. The results read cleanly against the baseline. The zone base rate scores nought point four one. A logistic regression with the as-of history features reaches nought point three six. The random forest reaches nought point three three, and histogram boosting nought point three one. Boosting and the forest are within about one fold standard deviation of each other, so accuracy alone barely separates them; but boosting fits seven times faster and is a fraction of the size. The logistic model gives up five hundredths of log loss in exchange for a model anyone can read end to end, which is a legitimate choice in some settings. And every number on this slide is a cross-validated score, which makes it selection evidence, not the final result.

Choosing a model and deciding how to use it are two halves of one recommendation. The first half is a trade-off between accuracy and cost. Plot every candidate by its cross-validated log loss and its prediction latency. The frontier joins the candidates that nothing else beats on both axes at once: the base rate, the logistic model and boosting. The forest sits behind the frontier, slower than boosting without being more accurate, so it drops out whatever the latency budget. Among the frontier models, the choice depends on how much accuracy is worth against speed and readability; here boosting is fast enough, and it is chosen. The second half is the decision policy, fixed on validation data before the test set is opened. Offer express shipping when the calibrated probability of lateness exceeds nought point three, the threshold that minimised expected cost in chapter seven. Never exceed two hundred offers per thousand orders, the courier's capacity. Abstain, and fall back to the carrier's standard promise, in any zone with less than ninety days of history. And keep a random five percent of flagged orders without intervention, so that labels stay honest.

With the pipeline, its calibration and the decision policy all fixed, the locked February and March test set is opened once. The useful way to present the result is as a ladder, with every number labelled by the kind of evidence it is. Training log loss is nought point two two, a training observation that says only that the model fits. The best cross-validated score is nought point three one, selection evidence, optimistic because it won. Nested cross-validation estimated the whole procedure at nought point three three. And the test result is nought point three two, inside the range the nested estimate predicted, which is what it looks like when an evaluation procedure has been honest. The cost at the chosen threshold, six hundred and twenty-eight pounds per thousand orders, is close to the six hundred and twenty-two seen on validation. Just as important is what the test cannot settle. Two months say nothing about seasons. West-zone recall of nought point four rests on twenty-five late orders. The effect of the express policy is measured by the holdout, not the test. And whether performance drifts later is a monitoring question for the MLOps course.

The model leaves this course not as a file but as a contract with engineering. The first part lists exactly what goes in at prediction time. Every field must be available at the checkout click, which is chapter one's rule, now enforced in code at the boundary. Each field states its type and two behaviours: what happens when it is missing, and what happens when it takes a value training never saw. A missing distance is imputed with the training median and flagged, exactly as the pipeline was trained. A missing zone or basket size rejects the request rather than guessing. A brand-new zone is encoded as all zeros, and the policy's abstain rule applies. A customer with no history at all takes an explicit new-customer path instead of a silent zero. The second part lists the artefacts that travel together and must never be separated: the fitted pipeline, the fitted calibrator, the policy configuration with its threshold, cap and abstain rule, the model card, the training data version, and the distribution of scores on the test set as a reference. How these are served, stored, monitored and retrained is the work of the MLOps course.

Across twelve chapters the course built three different kinds of thing, and the last lesson is that each is justified by its own kind of evidence. The late-risk model is supervised: it has labels, so it is judged by a locked final test, a log loss of nought point three two, together with its calibration and its recall in each subgroup. The customer segments are discovery: there are no labels at all, so they are judged by whether the same groups come back on resamples, a stability of nought point nine one, and then by whether the people who would use them can name them and act differently for each. The unusual-order detector sits between: its labels come only from reviewing the alerts it raises, so it is judged by the share of reviewed alerts that turned out to be real errors, thirty-one percent at fifty alerts a day. Evidence for one of these says nothing about another, and a report that mixes them is misleading. From here, practise on unfamiliar data, always writing the contract before the code. The MLOps course takes these artefacts into production; Deep Learning covers neural mechanisms; and Probability and Statistics covers experiments and causal questions.
